newsitem.title: USA: FDIC says bank lending standards solid.
newsitem.headline: FDIC says bank lending standards solid.

text.p: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. said Thursday loan underwriting standards at most of the banks it examined in recent months remained solid and unchanged from previous reviews.
"Very few of the banks the FDIC examined showed risky underwriting practices," FDIC Chairman Ricki Helfer said in a statement.

The report for April through September covered 1,383 institutions -- mostly banks and some savings and loans -- which represented 12 percent of all FDIC-insured firms and 6 percent of the assets, the FDIC said.
Ninety percent of the examinations showed no material change in underwriting practices, while 5 percent showed tighter practices and 5 percent reported looser practices.
FDIC examiners identified the effects of farm subsidy phaseouts as a potential concern at 40 percent of about 800 banks active in agricultural lending.
"The examiners are not reporting widespread problems although they're picking up isolated areas of potential concern," James Freund, an FDIC economist, said.

Twelve percent of the institutions were characterised by higher-than-normal risk in their lending practices, 28 percent frequently failed to adjust loan pricing based on loan quality and 11 percent of active construction lenders were cited for funding speculative projects, the FDIC said.

Almost all institutions active in credit card lending showed average or below-average underwriting risk for those loans, and none of the six banks that specialised in credit card lending showed notable weaknesses in current underwriting practices, the FDIC said.
Higher-than-normal risk in underwriting practices occurred most frequently at institutions with assets less than $25 million, the FDIC said.

Banks examined in the Boston and New York regions were rated as having less risky underwriting than elsewhere, while the San Francisco region continued to find a disproportionate number of institutions with above-average risk, the FDIC said.
